opus-5.5.text:
I think the comparison with GPT is really the clearest way to see it. When language models took off, the data problem had, in a sense, already been solved for us by history. Humanity spent decades putting text on the internet: books, forums, code, encyclopedias. All of that was sitting there, already digitized, already in a format the model could consume directly. The breakthrough was largely about finding the right architecture and the willingness to scale compute against a data pool that already existed.

Embodied intelligence doesn't have that inheritance. There is no "internet of physical interaction." Nobody has been uploading, for twenty years, the joint angles, forces, tactile signals, and camera views of every time they picked up a cup or folded a towel. That data simply was never recorded, because before robots there was no reason to record it. So we're starting much closer to zero.

And it's not just a matter of quantity. The data is also much harder to collect and much harder to reuse. With text, one sentence is useful to everyone. With robot data, a trajectory collected on one arm with one gripper and one camera setup doesn't transfer cleanly to a different body. The embodiment gap fragments the data. Collection is also expensive: you need hardware, operators doing teleoperation, real environments, resets, safety. You can't just scrape it.

People often say, well, use simulation, or use human videos. Those help, and I think they're important pieces. But simulation has the sim-to-real gap, especially for contact and deformable objects, and videos of humans give you the visual "what" but not the action-level "how," the forces, the precise control signals. So each source covers part of the problem, but none of them is the equivalent of the web for language.

So my view is that for embodied AI, model architecture matters, but the defining question for the next several years is: how do we build a data engine? How do we get diverse, high-quality, scalable interaction data, and how do we design models that can absorb heterogeneous sources, real robots, simulation, human video, and actually get something like a scaling law out of it? Until that's answered, data will remain the bottleneck, in a way it never really was for GPT.

r001.rationale: The response says internet text enabled language models and that embodied intelligence lacks equivalent interaction data, but it does not identify substantial internet-data use in pretraining an embodied-specific model.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the decades of digitized internet text already available to language models with embodied intelligence starting close to zero and lacking recorded robot interactions, conveying a much larger available internet-data pool.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that GPT got to ride on a data source that already existed, and embodied intelligence doesn't have one.

When language models took off, the internet had already spent two or three decades accumulating text. Trillions of tokens, written by humans, for humans, sitting there essentially for free. The research question was mostly about compute and architecture, because the data problem had been solved by accident. Same story with images and video: people uploaded billions of them, and vision models inherited that.

Robotics has no equivalent. There is no internet of robot trajectories. Nobody spent twenty years recording joint angles, gripper forces, and camera streams while folding laundry. So every lab that wants to train a policy has to go generate the data itself, and that is slow, expensive, and hardware-specific. A dataset collected on one arm with one gripper and one camera setup often transfers poorly to a different robot. Text doesn't have that problem. A sentence is a sentence regardless of which keyboard typed it.

There is also a question of what the data actually contains. Text is a compressed record of human thought, so a model trained on it absorbs a lot of world knowledge indirectly. Robot data is mostly about physical interaction: contact, friction, deformation, what happens when you push something slightly too hard. That information is barely written down anywhere, because humans never needed to articulate it. We learned it in our bodies. So you can't recover it from the web, you have to go collect it.

People try to shortcut this in a few ways. Teleoperation gives you high-quality demonstrations but scales with human hours. Simulation scales well but you pay in realism, and the gap between sim and real contact physics is still real. Human video from the internet is abundant but the embodiment is wrong, you have to bridge from a human hand to a robot gripper. Each of those helps, and I think the eventual answer is a mixture, but none of them individually gives you the clean flywheel that text gave language models.

That is why I keep calling data the bottleneck rather than models. If someone handed us a hundred billion diverse, well-labeled robot interactions tomorrow, I believe the architectures we already have would do remarkably well. We don't have that, and getting there is the actual work of the next several years.

r001.rationale: The response says internet text and images helped language and vision models, but does not identify substantial internet-data use to pretrain a model designed specifically for embodied intelligence.

r002.rationale: It contrasts trillions of internet text tokens and billions of uploaded images and videos with the lack of an equivalent internet-scale source of robot trajectories.

astra-6.text:
I think the key difference is where the data comes from. For GPT, there was already a huge amount of text on the internet. People had spent decades producing it, and much of it could be used directly for training. For embodied intelligence, we don’t have an equivalent collection of robots interacting with the physical world.

You can learn a lot from images and videos, but watching someone pick up a cup doesn’t tell you exactly what force they applied, what they felt through contact, or how they corrected their movement when the cup slipped. Those are precisely the things a robot needs to learn. Collecting that experience requires hardware, time, and often human supervision.

And the diversity matters as much as the volume. A skill that works with one object in one room may fail with a different object or a different robot. So collecting more repetitions in a controlled setting doesn’t necessarily solve generalization.

Simulation can help, but then you have to ask whether what the robot learns transfers to reality, especially for contact and manipulation. That’s why I see data as a continuing bottleneck: we need a scalable way to collect diverse, useful interaction experience, not just larger models.

r001.rationale: The response says GPT used abundant internet text, but does not say internet data was used to pretrain a model designed specifically for embodied intelligence.

r002.rationale: It contrasts a huge amount of available internet text with the lack of an equivalent collection of robots interacting with the physical world, conveying that internet data is available at a much greater scale.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key difference is where the data comes from. For GPT, there was already an enormous amount of text on the internet, produced by people over many years. You could collect that data and train a model without first building a system to generate every example.

For embodied intelligence, we don’t have an equivalent supply of interaction data. A robot needs to learn how its actions change the physical world—what happens when it grasps something, how much force to apply, and how to recover when it fails. Images and videos provide useful information, but they usually don’t contain the actions, forces, or feedback needed to learn those behaviors directly.

Collecting that experience on real robots is slow and expensive. And the variation is huge: a small change in the object, the environment, or the robot itself can change what works. Simulation helps, but transferring what you learn into the real world remains a challenge.

So the bottleneck isn’t simply having more images or more hours of video. It’s obtaining diverse, useful interaction experience at scale. We still need a data-generation process that can grow alongside the models.

r001.rationale: The response says GPT was trained on abundant internet text, but it does not state that internet data was used to pretrain a model designed specifically for embodied intelligence.

r002.rationale: It contrasts an enormous supply of internet text with the lack of an equivalent supply of robot interaction data, communicating that internet data is available at much greater scale.
